beats.intro: Lesson thirty. [[sub]]How pay can carry task-relevant feedback: the performance bonus and the base salary.
beats.money: Money matters at every level of the need hierarchy. [[need]]Lower down, it buys food, housing and insurance. It meets physical and security needs. [[meas]]Higher up, it becomes a measure of your worth among others. [[test]]Remember the raise test. [[abs]]If the dollar amount of a raise is what matters, money is a need. [[rel]]If what matters is how it compares with what others got, money is a measure.
beats.middle: Where do middle managers sit? [[paid]]In Grove's experience, they are paid well enough that money is not crucial to them, [[notyet]]but not so well that it means nothing. [[differ]]And needs differ a lot from person to person: children or none, a working spouse or not. [[empathy]]So be sensitive to each person's money needs, and show empathy. [[project]]Above all, don't project your own circumstances onto others.
beats.hard: As managers, we want high performance. [[feed]]So we want to use money as task-relevant feedback. [[tie]]That means tying pay to performance. [[but]]But performance is hard to judge precisely. [[piece]]A middle manager can't be paid by the piece; the job is never simple output. [[team]]And their work is woven into the work of a team. So a pay scheme tied directly to one manager's own performance is hard to design.
beats.bonus: Grove's compromise: base part of the pay on performance. [[name]]Call it a performance bonus. [[rise]]The bonus share should rise with total pay. [[senior]]For a highly paid senior manager, the extra dollars matter little, so the bonus can be as much as half of total pay. [[mid]]For a middle manager, more like ten to twenty-five percent. [[taste]]Big swings at that level could cause real hardship. But even a smaller share gives a taste of task-relevant feedback.
beats.design: Designing a bonus raises four questions. [[who]]First, is the performance a team's or mostly one person's? And if a team, which one: a project, a division, the whole company? [[when]]Second, what period should it cover? Cause and effect are often far apart, yet the bonus must come soon enough that people remember why they got it. [[what]]Third, what is it based on: countable results, measurable objectives, or subjective judgment, which can turn into a beauty contest? [[broke]]And fourth, it must not pay out lavishly while the company heads for bankruptcy.
beats.three: Take all that into account and the scheme gets complicated. [[ex]]Here is Grove's example. [[twenty]]Take twenty percent of a manager's pay, and split it three ways. [[ind]]One part for individual performance, judged by the supervisor. [[dept]]One for the immediate team's objective results, perhaps the department. [[corp]]One for the company's overall financial results. [[small]]Each part moves total pay only a little, yet each draws attention. [[spot]]No scheme gives exactly what you want. But most will spotlight performance.
beats.base: Now base salaries. In the abstract, there are two pure ways to set them. [[exp]]Experience only: pay rises with time in the job. [[max]]But every job has a maximum value, so the curve must level off. [[merit]]Merit only: time doesn't count. I don't care if you are one year out of college or twenty years in, only how you perform in this job. [[cap]]Here too, the job has a maximum value.
beats.routine: Social norms can push us into poor practice. [[over]]We say every job has a limit, then keep giving routine raises until someone is paid too much for it. [[pure]]And many organizations use experience only. [[japan]]Large Japanese companies, as Grove described them, made no performance distinction for the first ten years or so, probably the most productive years of a career. [[union]]Unions and most government jobs lean the same way. [[teach]]Take teachers in many school systems. A good one and a bad one with the same years are paid the same. [[msg]]Fair or not, the message is that performance doesn't matter much. Grove even wonders if pass-fail grading came from the way teachers are paid.
beats.compromise: Pure merit is impractical, too. It is very hard to ignore experience when you try to pay fairly. [[fam]]So most companies choose a compromise: a family of curves, each shaped like the experience curve. [[start]]People start at the same level, [[speed]]rise at different speeds, [[arrive]]and arrive at different places, depending on their performance.
beats.rank: Experience only is the easiest to run. [[book]]If someone dislikes their raise, you show them the book: so much time in the job, so much pay. [[finite]]With merit or a compromise, you are dividing a finite pot of money, and that takes thought and effort. [[compare]]It also needs a competitive, comparative evaluation of people. Many managers find that troubling. [[last]]If someone is first, someone else has to be last. [[race]]We accept that in a race. Even the runner who finishes last accepts the system. [[work]]At work, ranking is highly charged, hard to accept and to run. But it is a must if salary is to encourage performance.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Money is a need lower down, a measure higher up. Don't project your own circumstances. [[w2]]The bonus share rises with pay: up to half for senior managers. [[w3]]Decide whose performance, what period, what basis, and protect the company. [[w4]]Base pay: experience only, merit only, or the usual compromise. [[w5]]Merit pay needs honest ranking: someone is first, someone last. Now the lesson practice.

beats.finish: Well done. That is the end of lesson thirty.
